EdgeCase is a Python library for building, analyzing, querying, and drawing graphs. Its algorithms
run in a Rust core, so they stay fast on graphs with millions of edges, while its interface is
plain Python: you build a graph with a few method calls, compute what you need, and get the results
back as ordinary dictionaries and lists or as Polars DataFrames.

```{python}
import edgecase as ec

graph = ec.karate_club().pagerank().cmty_louvain()
graph
```

That one line loads Zachary's karate club network, scores every member with PageRank, and divides
the club into communities. The printed summary describes the graph and lists the two computations
that have been stored on it. The rest of this guide explains each part of that line, and much more
besides.

## What EdgeCase provides

EdgeCase covers the whole life of a graph, from building it to publishing a figure of it:

- **Construction.** Add nodes and edges one at a time or in bulk, build a graph from a list of
  pairs or from Polars DataFrames, generate one from nearly a hundred models (grids,
  trees, random graphs, small worlds, scale-free networks, community benchmarks), or load one of
  the bundled datasets.
- **Analysis.** Hundreds of algorithms: paths and distances, centrality, community detection,
  clustering and motifs, connectivity and flows, spanning trees, DAG analysis, similarity and link
  prediction, spectral methods, coloring, matching, isomorphism, percolation, and influence
  spreading.
- **Data access.** Every node and edge can carry attributes, and the whole graph can be viewed as
  a pair of Polars DataFrames for filtering, joining, and summarizing.
- **Selection and traversal.** Select nodes or edges by attribute, degree, centrality or pattern,
  walk outward from a selection along edges, and then act on whatever is selected.
- **Querying.** Find shapes in a graph with a subset of Cypher, the query language of Neo4j, and
  get the matches back as a DataFrame.
- **Visualization.** Draw static SVG figures with `plot()`, explore large graphs in interactive
  widgets, compute layouts, and map attributes to colors and sizes.
- **Provenance.** Every change to a graph is recorded in a step log, which can be inspected,
  exported, or replayed as an animation.
- **Interoperability.** Read and write more than twenty file formats, and convert to and from
  NetworkX, igraph, NumPy, SciPy, and pandas.

## Three ideas that run through the library

A few conventions appear in nearly every method. Learning them early makes the rest of the API
predictable.

**Nodes have IDs and labels.** Each node gets an integer ID, assigned in order from 1, and may
have a string label that you choose. Wherever a method takes a node, an integer means an ID and a
string means a label. So both of these refer to the karate club's instructor, whose label is
`"0"`:

```{python}
graph.get_node(1)
```

```{python}
graph.get_node("0")
```

**Methods chain.** Methods that build, change, or annotate a graph return the graph itself, so
calls can be strung together into a pipeline that reads top to bottom.

**Results are stored on the graph by default.** Methods that compute a value for every node, such
as a centrality score or a community, write it to a node attribute named after the method and hand
back the graph. Ask for `return_dict=True` to get a dictionary keyed by node ID instead:

```{python}
ranks = graph.pagerank(return_dict=True)
round(ranks[1], 4)
```

Stored attributes show up as columns of the node table, which makes it easy to compare several
measures side by side:

```{python}
graph.get_node_df().sort("pagerank", descending=True)
```

## How this guide is organized

The guide moves from the basics to specialized topics, and each page can be read on its own once
the first few are familiar.

- **Getting started** covers installation and a [quick tour](02-quick-start.qmd) of the library.
- **Building graphs** explains the [graph model](03-graph-model.qmd), the
  [construction methods](04-building-graphs.qmd), [generators](05-generators.qmd), and the
  [bundled datasets](06-datasets.qmd).
- **Working with graphs** covers [node and edge data](07-node-and-edge-data.qmd),
  [selections](08-selections.qmd), [traversals](09-traversals.qmd), and
  [Cypher queries](10-cypher.qmd).
- **Analysis** works through the algorithm families, from
  [structural properties](11-structure.qmd) and [paths](12-paths.qmd) to
  [centrality](13-centrality.qmd), [communities](14-communities.qmd), and beyond.
- **Visualization** covers [static plots](22-plotting.qmd), [layouts](23-layouts.qmd),
  [aesthetics](24-aesthetics.qmd), [interactive widgets](25-interactive.qmd), and the
  [step log](26-step-log.qmd).
- **Interoperability** covers [file formats](27-file-formats.qmd),
  [other libraries](28-other-libraries.qmd), and [summary tables](29-tables.qmd).
- **Specialized topics** cover [multiplex networks](30-multiplex.qmd),
  [network biology](31-network-biology.qmd), and [spreading and robustness](32-spreading.qmd).

Each page links to the [API reference](../reference/index.qmd) for the methods it uses, where every
parameter is documented in full.
